background.definition: Endometriosis is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside the endometrial cavity such as in the ovaries, peritoneum, uterosacral ligaments, pouch of Douglas, and rarely extra pelvic deposits.

list.listitem: A large retrospective Kaiser Permanente study reported an average incidence of 24.3 cases per 10,000 person-years and prevalence rate of 1.9% among the US population. Incidence rate was similar across race and ethnicities.

However, a meta-analysis of 18 studies showed that black women appeared to be less likely to be diagnosed with endometriosis (odds ratio [OR] 0.49; 95% CI 0.29-0.83) and Asian women were slightly more likely to carry this diagnosis (OR 1.63; 95% CI 1.03-2.58).
An incidence rate of 3.5 per 1000 was found in a German health insurance database of 62,323 women.

A much lower average annual incidence rate of 7.2 per 10,000 (95% CI 6.5-8.0) was reported using databases of Maccabi Healthcare Services (MHS), a 2-million-member healthcare provider representing one quarter of the Israeli population.

Among 495 U.S. women undergoing laparoscopy/laparotomy, endometriosis incidence was 0.7% by histology only, 7% by MRI, and 41% by visualization. MRI-diagnosed endometriosis in a matched population cohort of 131 women was 11%.
Overall prevalence is 10% to 15% of women of reproductive age.
In a systematic review of adolescents with chronic pelvic pain who underwent laparoscopy, a high prevalence of endometriosis was noted in 64% of individuals.

A large prospective population-based study from Israel showed a prevalence rate of 18.6 per 1000 (95% CI 17.7-19.5) in women aged 40 to 44 years, with an infertility rate of 37% among them. However, point prevalence of endometriosis was much lower at 10.8 per 1000 (95% CI 10.5-11.0).
In the German study above, the standardized prevalence rate was low at 8.1 per 1000 women. The highest prevalence rate in this study was 12.8/1000 observed among women aged 35 to 44 years.

Estimates of total direct costs ranged from $1109 per patient per year in Canada to $12118 per patient per year in the US. Indirect costs of endometriosis ranged from $3314 per patient per year in Austria to $15737 per patient per year in the US.

A meta-analysis including large cohort and case-control studies showed that women with endometriosis had an increased risk of both endometrial cancer (RR 1.662, 95% C, 1.148-2.407) and breast cancer (RR 1.082, 95% CI 1.001-1.169). Among ovarian cancers, the strongest risk was for clear cell (SRR 3.44, 95% CI 2.82-4.42; n = 5 studies) and endometrioid (SRR 2.33, 95% CI 1.82-2.98; n = 5 studies) histotypes, although significant evidence of both heterogeneity across studies and publication bias was found.

This increased ovarian cancer risk was also seen in a cohort of over 21,000 women undergoing infertility treatment in Australia, in which women diagnosed with endometriosis who remained nulliparous had an increased risk of ovarian cancer (hazard ratio [HR] 3.1; 95% CI 1.1-8.6). The HR did not reach significance in parous women with endometriosis. The risk appears highest among women with tissue-proven ovarian endometrioma, especially for endometrioid (4.72 [2.75-7.56]) and clear cell (10.1 [5.50-16.9]) ovarian cancer.
One-sided oophorectomy and radical extirpation of all visible endometriosis appear to be protective against later development of ovarian cancer.

Endometriosis-associated malignant transformation in an abdominal surgical scar, primarily from cesarean section, is rare but aggressive. Authors of a systematic review of 48 cases, including one from their own institution, found clear-cell carcinoma to be the most prevalent histology (67%) followed by endometrioid adenocarcinoma (15%); five-year survival was about 40%. Interestingly, in another study, 27% of deep infiltrating endometriotic lesions from 27 patients harbored somatic cancer driver mutations.
There is evidence of subclinical atherosclerosis in women with endometriosis which can regress after surgical removal of endometriosis.

Significantly increased risk of ischemic heart disease (HR 1.50, 95%CI 1.37-1.65; I2 = 0 %) and cerebrovascular disease (HR 1.17, 95%CI 1.07-1.29; I2 = 0 %) was associated with endometriosis in a recent meta-analysis.
There was a significant association between endometriosis and risk of migraine headache in a recent meta-analysis (OR 1.56, 95% CI 1.21-1.90).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 24 studies including 99,614 women found higher levels of depression among women with endometriosis compared to controls (standardized mean difference 0.22; 95% CI 0.13-0.32); however, there was no difference in depression between women with pelvic pain and endometriosis vs. those with pelvic pain without endometriosis.
Graves' disease , but not hypothyroidism, is associated with endometriosis (OR 2.52; 95% CI 1.30-4.88).
Endometriosis increases the risk of gestational diabetes (OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.07-1.51) based on a meta-analysis of 18 studies involving 4,600,885 women.
The cause of ectopic deposits of endometrial tissue is multifactorial and includes mechanical, genetic, hormonal, immune mediated and microbiome-associated factors.

There are several theories proposed to explain the pathogenesis. The most widely held Sampson's theory of retrograde reflux of menstrual tissue from the fallopian tubes during menstruation; other theories are coelomic metaplastic theory, the vascular and lymphatic metastatic theory and microtrauma due to uterine hyperperistalsis. The well-supported molecular hallmarks of genetic predisposition, estrogen dependence, progesterone resistance and inflammation are known.
Ectopic endometriotic implants are believed to recruit their own neural and vascular supplies through neuroangiogenesis.

Regulatory T cells were found to be decreased in both ectopic endometrium as well the endometrium of women with endometriosis. The authors postulated that this T-cell deficiency exaggerates local inflammation and angiogenesis and simultaneously facilitates attachment and growth of endometrial implants.

MicroRNA, single-stranded RNAs that regulate gene expression at the post-transcriptional level, appear to play a role in endometriosis development. In one case-control study, endometriosis-derived microRNAs collected from sera were shown to regulate macrophage cytokine production that contribute to inflammation associated with this endometriosis.
Vascular endothelial growth factor, its major subtype (VEGF-A) and associated receptor (VEGFR-2) were significantly increased indeep endometriosis lesions.

Genetic predisposition: Associations have been found with interleukin-10-592 A/C polymorphisms. Other susceptibility loci for endometriosis include Rs1333049 risk allele G and rs7521902. Genotype at rs11977660, a single-nucleotide polymorphism of epidermal growth factor receptor, was significantly associated with endometriosis in a Chinese case-control study. There is an association between ADAMTS13/vWF and the risk of endometriosis based on GWAS data from large-scale population studies.

Significant genetic correlations between endometriosis and 11 pain conditions, including migraine, back and multisite chronic pain, as well as inflammatory conditions such as asthma and osteoarthritis have been observed.

Endocannabinoid modulators appear to affect specific mechanisms involved in endometriosis establishment and maintenance. The picture is far from clear as selective cannabinoid receptor agonists have a favorable action in limiting cell proliferation and pain symptoms but also stimulate endometrial cell migration.

A significant correlation between CA-125 and CA 19-9 with dehydroepiandrosterone- DHEA-S (R = 0.52 and R = 0.49) was demonstrated in women with endometriosis suggesting that androgens may play a role in endometrium-related cancer pathology in women with endometriosis.
There is an association between endometriosis and increased proteobacteria, enterobacteriaceae, streptococcus and Escherichia coli across various microbiome sites.
Endometriosis is believed to impair fertility by inducing a local inflammatory state and progesterone resistance, impairing oocyte release, and interfering with sperm and embryo transport.

list.listitem: Higher intake of dairy foods may be protective against endometriosis. In the Nurses’ Health Study, women who reported consuming more than 3 servings of total dairy foods per day were 18% less likely to be diagnosed with endometriosis than those reporting 2 servings per day (rate ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.71-0.95).

Breast feeding may be protective (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.90-0.94 for every additional three months of total breast feeding per pregnancy). The association was only partly explained by postpartum amenorrhea.
Continuous oral contraceptives, newer progestin (Dienogest), and the LNG-IUD may prevent recurrence in women with endometriosis who had conservative surgery.

Authors of a Cochrane review found post-surgical hormone suppression may benefit pain and reduce disease recurrence, but there is insufficient evidence regardng pre-surgical hormone suppression therapy.

Based on 4 RCTs with 157 subjects who underwent laparoscopic surgery for symptomatic endometriosis, Cochrane authors could not determine if there was improvement in dysmenorrhea or quality of life at 12 months with post‐operative use of LNG‐IUD. Two studies were ongoing at the time of this review and quality of evidence was rated as very low to low.
Diagnosis is usually based on typical presentation; individual signs and symptoms, while specific, are not sensitive. C
Transvaginal ultrasound is reasonably accurate and considered first-line diagnostic testing. C
Definitive diagnosis is best made using direct visualization with histologic confirmation. C

list.listitem: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends direct visualization of ectopic endometrial lesions accompanied by histologic confirmation.

Four stages defined by the American Society of Reproductive Medicine are used to describe the severity of endometriosis based on a point system. The stages do not correlate with symptom severity, although infertility is likely in patients with stage IV disease. Descriptively, these stages are: Stage I, minimal (restricted to superficial lesions although possibly some adhesions) Stage II, mild (some deep lesions present in cul-de-sac, superficial ovarian endometriosis) Stage III, moderate (above plus presence of deep ovarian endometriomas and adhesions) Stage IV, severe (large endometriomas and extensive adhesions)
Patients most often present with cyclical pain at the time of menses, with or without infertility.

No individual sign or symptom is particularly sensitive for the diagnosis of endometriosis; however pain is the most sensitive symptom (56%). The ACOG committee opinion on dysmenorrhea in the adolescent recommends that endometriosis be considered in patients with persistent, clinically significant dysmenorrhea despite treatment with hormonal agents and nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, particularly if no other etiology for chronic pelvic pain or secondary dysmenorrhea has been identified based on history, physical examination, and pelvic ultrasonography.
Premenstrual spotting of ≥2 days is strongly associated with histologically confirmed endometriosis in women with infertility (OR 16; 95% CI 3.9-65.4).
Useful predictors of stage III or IV endometriosis in one study were menstrual dyschezia (difficulty defecating) and a history of benign ovarian cysts (area under the curve, 84.9).
The main symptoms suggestive of endometriosis are: severe dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, painful defecation during menstruation, urinary tract symptoms during menstruation, and infertility.

In one small case series of 37 women treated for abdominal endometriosis, a palpable abdominal mass was the most common initial finding (97.2%). In a second case series of 65 patients, abdominal pain was the primary clinical presentation for 73.8% and/or a mass/lump in 63.1%. In the latter study, most women (81.5%) had a history of cesarean section.
Among 25 women with rectosigmoid endometriosis, incomplete evacuation was the most common symptom.

Endometriosis may rarely present as ascites; in these cases, abdominal distention, anorexia/weight loss, abdominal pain, and menometrorrhagia are the most common clinical symptoms and pelvic mass is the most common physical finding.

Menstrual stigma, variability in presenting symptoms, difficulty in establishing pathological symptoms from normal menstruation and lack of training of health care professionals are the barriers leading to delay in diagnosis of endometriosis.

Authors of a systematic review and comparative analysis of 5 national (ACOG, 2010; Collège National des Gynécologues et Obstétriciens Français, 2006; European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology, 2014; National German Guideline, 2014; The Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada, 2010) and two international guidelines (World Endometriosis Society, 2013 and Australasian CREI Consensus Expert Panel on Trial Evidence, 2012) found 4 consistent recommendations on diagnosis from national guidelines, 3 consistent medical treatment recommendations and one surgical recommendations. With respect to diagnosis, transvaginal ultrasound was recommended for diagnosis of endometrioma, histology was recommended for diagnosis of mild-moderate endometriosis and to confirm the diagnosis of endometriosis, and the use of biomarkers was not recommended.

Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is accurate for the diagnosis of pelvic endometriosis, deep pelvic endometriosis, or intestinal involvement of endometriosis; for intestinal involvement, a systematic review found LR+ of 30.36 (4.8-48.56) and LR− of 0.09 (0.02-0.36).

A meta-analysis of 4 studies, comprising 560 patients, showed TVUS has high specificity of 98% (95% CI 95–99%), but low sensitivity of 31% (95% CI 10–64%) for detection of parametrial deep endometriosis.

In another study of deep infiltrative endometriosis among 317 patients with signs and symptoms of endometriosis who underwent laparoscopy and histopathologic exam, both TVUS and transrectal US had reasonably high sensitivity (83.3% and 80.5%, respectively) but low specificity (46.1% and 18.6%, respectively) compared to MRI (90.4% sensitivity and 66.1% specificity).

However, the diagnostic performance of TVUS and MRI is similar for detecting deep infiltrating endometriosis involving rectosigmoid, uterosacral ligaments and rectovaginal septum based on a meta-analysis of six studies (n = 424).

In a study of patients scheduled for laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis, MR colonography had very high accuracy in detecting colorectal involvement. In another study of patients with deep infiltrating endometriosis, both TVUS and contrast-enhanced MR-colonography were similarly sensitive and specific, with LR+ of 13.9 and 24.4, respectively and LR− of 0.2 and 0.3, respectively. Finally, in a recent study, 3.0-T MR enterography had high sensitivity and specificity for bowel endometriosis (92-96 and 100%, respectively).
If definitive diagnosis is desired, it is best made with direct visualization using laparoscopy.
The presence of nerve fibers in an endometrial biopsy specimen had high sensitivity (98%) and specificity (83%) for laparoscopy-proven endometriosis.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that none of the 22 biomarkers evaluated, including anti-endometrial antibodies and CA-125, differentiated women with endometriosis from disease-free controls. Combinations of biomarkers were also found to be unhelpful.

In a recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 observational studies, CA-125 was highly specific (93%; 95% CI 89%-95%) but had low sensitivity (52%; 95% CI 38%-66%); about half the women with histologically-proven endometriosis had normal CA-125 levels.

Women with endometriosis have higher serum levels of inflammatory markers and reduced expression of microRNA than women without endometriosis. In one study, combined use of serum microRNA-17 and interleukin 4 and 6 serum levels resulted in an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.79 to 0.84 for endometriosis.

Serum intercellular adhesion molecule-1 has a sensitivity and specificity for endometriosis of 0.65 (95% CI 0.52-0.75) and 0.78 (95% CI 0.62-0.89), with an AUC of the overall analysis of 0.76 (0.72-0.80); diagnostic accuracy was highest among women of Asian ethnicity.
There may be a correlation between elevated serum and peritoneal fluid IL-6 concentrations and the occurrence of endometriosis-associated infertility.
Other causes of pelvic pain such as PID, primary dysmenorrhea, ovarian cysts, and fibroids should be excluded.
Empiric diagnosis based on clinical presentation is reasonable.
Patients with persistent symptoms after empiric treatment and inconclusive pelvic ultrasound should be referred for laparoscopy.
Treatment should be directed towards symptom relief, suppression of disease progression, and protection of future fertility.
Beneficial treatments for pain are combined oral contraceptives (OCs), oral or intramuscular progesterone, LNG-IUD, GnRH analogues, laparoscopic ablation, and excision. A
OC's are used to relieve dysmenorrhea with endometrial implants less than 5 cm, while oral or intramuscular medroxyprogesterone provide pain relief for deep infiltrating lesions. B
It is not clear if postoperative use of LNG-IUD reduces recurrence of painful menses or improves quality of life. B
Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogs may reduce endometriosis-associated pain but have uncertain effects on recurrence, and use is limited by side effects and cost. A

GnRH analogue use for 3 months and laparoscopic ablation or excision are associated with increased pregnancy rates in women with endometriosis, but data are insufficient for confirming an increase in clinical pregnancy rates. B GnRH analogue use for 6 months after surgery for endometriosis may reduce recurrence risk.

Laparoscopic surgery with ablation of endometrial deposits appears to increase fertility (clinical pregnancy rates) and live birth rates but it is uncertain if it reduces overall pain in mild to severe endometriosis. B
Empiric use of NSAIDS or acetaminophen is a reasonable first-line treatment, but there is insufficient supporting evidence.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 17 high-quality Cohrane reviews on endometriosis and a systematic review published in JAMA by the same authors concluded that while data on NSAIDs are inconclusive, beneficial treatments for pain are LNG-IUD, GnRH analogues, laparoscopic ablation, and excision. GnRH analogues for 3 months and laparoscopic ablation or excision are associated with increased pregnancy rates in women with endometriosis, but the authors were not able to confirm an increase in clinical pregnancy rates. Combined OCs, progesterone, GnRH analogues and elagolix are the best for reducing dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain and dyspareunia when ranked among patients with endometriosis.

It is not clear if combined OCs provide pain relief according to the Cochrane database, but a subsequent systematic review and meta-analysis of 36 RCTs supports the use of OCs as one of the methods for pain relief in patients with endometriosis. Guidelines are consistent on recommending combined OCs for endometriosis-associated pain.
In a small case series of 26 women with colorectal endometriosis, continuous OC use was followed by reduced endometriosis symptoms including bowel-related symptoms.
Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence of benefit on pain, recurrence, or pregnancy rate for pre- or post-surgical hormone suppression therapy.

However, authors of a meta-analysis 3 RCTs and one cohort study of 557 women with endometriosis who were treated surgically for endometriomas found lower recurrence rates for dysmenorrhea with continuous vs. cyclic OCs postoperatively (RR 0.24; 95% CI 0.06-0.91). There were no differences for chronic pelvic pain or dyspareunia.
Guidelines are consistent on recommending progestogens for endometriosis-associated pain.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 13 studies concluded that both intramuscular progesterone 150 mg monthly (Depo-Provera) and oral medroxyprogesterone acetate (100 mg daily) were more effective than placebo and comparable to other treatments for symptomatic improvement but associated with increased side effects, with higher rates of acne and edema (vs. placebo) and amenorrhea and bleeding (vs. other active treatment) for oral treatment.14

In an RCT of 84 women with symptomatic endometriosis undergoing conservative surgery, both postoperative Depo-Provera and postoperative OCs improved pain over 24 weeks and were comparable for high patient satisfaction. Dysmenorrhea scores on a visual analog scale were significantly higher in the OC group.

Cochrane authors could not determine if there was improvement in dysmenorrhea or quality of life at 12 months with LNG IUD use for symptomatic endometriosis following surgery. Two studies were ongoing at the time of this review and quality of evidence was rated as very low to low.

The LNG-IUD did not appear to be effective for preventing endometrioma recurrence at 30 months in one small RCT of 80 women (25% in the intervention group vs. 37.5% in the control group), although there was a lower dysmenorrhea recurrence rate in the IUD group (NNT = 5)

Mifeprestone , a progesterone antagonist, relieves dysmenorrhea based on moderate quality evidence, although there was a lower dysmenorrhea recurrence rate in the IUD group (NNT = 5). Low-quality evidence suggests that this agent relieves dyspareunia. In one RCT, mifepristone changed baseline VAS scores (0 - 10, with 10 indicating the most severe pain) by –6.63 points compared to placebo –0.95 points in premenopausal women, aged 18 to 50 years, with adenomyosis and associated dysmenorrhea in a RCT.
Progesterone receptor modulator mifeprisonte relieves dysmenorrhoea supported by moderate quality evidence, and low-quality evidence suggests that this agent relieves dyspareunia.
Guidelines are consistent on recommending GnRH analogs for endometriosis-associated pain.

Based on many small trials, GnRH analogs provide better pain relief than placebo and equivalent pain relief as levonorgestrel or danazol but have significant hypoestrogenic side effects (e.g., hot flushes). These medications are expensive.

In an RCT, hormonal add-back therapy with 5 mg/d norethindrone acetate plus 0.625 mg/d conjugated equine estrogens preserved bone health and improved quality of life, for adolescents and young women with endometriosis during 12 months of GnRH agonist therapy.

Authors of a Cochrane review of small RCTs showed decrease in overall pain, reported as pelvic pain scores (RR 2.14, 95% CI 1.41 to 3.24, low-certainty evidence), dysmenorrhea scores (RR 2.25, 95% CI 1.59 to 3.16, low-certainty evidence), dyspareunia scores (RR 2.21, 95% CI 1.39 to 3.54, low-certainty evidence), and pelvic tenderness scores (RR 2.28, 95% CI 1.48 to 3.50, low-certainty evidence) after three months of treatment with GnRH analogs..

Using a Markov model for endometriosis disease course, the use of a GnRH agonist for 6 months following laparoscopic or open surgery for endometriosis was cost effective for the prevention of endometriosis recurrence compared with no therapy with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio ranging from $6,185 per quality-adjusted life year in deep endometriosis to $6,425 with peritoneal endometriosis.

Authors of a network meta-analysis of the RCTs involving expectant management, cyclic OC, continuous OC, GnRHa and GnRHa + LNG-IUS found that all hormonal regimens had a nonsignificant lower risk of endometrioma recurrence compared with expectant management.

Oral GnRH antagonists such as elagolix 400 mg and ASP1707 15 mg are effective in reducing pelvic pain, dyspareunia and dysmenorrhea, although relugolix 40 mg may be best in reducing pain. Headache, hot flashes (elagolix 250 and relugolix 40 mg) and decreased BMD (elagolix 250 mg) are reported.

Long term oral use of elagolix (GnRH antagonist) over 12 months at doses of 150 mg daily or 200 mg twice daily resulted in meaningful reduction of dysmenorrohea at the rate of 67.5% and 69.1%, respectively, in 2 extension studies. In addition, rates of dyspareunia reduction were 45.2% at 150 mg once daily and 60.0% at 200 mg twice daily. The most common adverse effect was hot flushes. Decreases from baseline in bone mineral density and increases from baseline in lipids were also reported.
Danazol provides pain relief over placebo but has significant androgenic side effects.

Aromatase inhibitors: Good clinical efficiency is observed when combined with hormonal treatment for disease control making this a good treatment option for postmenopausal women when surgery is contraindicated.
Pentoxifylline: Based on 5 RCTs, there is no effect of pentoxifylline (immune modulator with anti-inflammatory effects) on pain or clinical pregnancy rates.

Anti-angiogenic therapy : Experimental studies of several anti-angiogenic agents (e.g., growth factor inhibitors) showed regression of endometrial lesions by reducing their blood supply. Elevated levels of ERβ and GPER are found in endometriotic tissue compared to normal tissue, and could serve as new molecular therapeutic targets to suppress endometriosis-specific angiogenesis. In a single small trial of infliximab (an anti-TNF-α drug), the drug was not effective for endometriosis-related pelvic pain reduction vs. placebo.

Postoperative Hormone Suppression : Various hormone treatment such as combined hormonal contraceptives (6 studies, n = 869), progestin (3 studies, n = 183), LNG-IUS (2 studies, n = 94) and GnRH agonist (9 studies, n = 1237) post operatively for one year after surgery, reduces pain and recurrence (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.65] based on a meta-analysis.

Laparoscopic surgery and removal of endometrial deposits compared to diagnostic laparascopy alone, results in improved pain outcomes for women with endometriosis; there was no defenitive conclusion about its usefulness in women with severe disease. In addition, ablation of endometrial deposits with or without uterine nerve ablation decreases pain.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 14 RCTs concluded that it is uncertain whether laparoscopic surgery reduces overall pain associated with minimal to severe endometriosis compared to diagnostic laparoscopy only. No data were reported on live birth. There is moderate quality evidence that laparoscopic surgery increases viable intrauterine pregnancy rates confirmed by ultrasound compared to diagnostic laparoscopy only.

Laparoscopic surgery with excision has a more favorable outcome than drainage and ablation of ovarian endometriomata, in terms of recurrence of pain, endometrioma and subsequent spontaneous pregnancy in women who were previously subfertile. Laparoscopic electrocautery of the endometrioma wall may be an alternative.
Improvement of fertility after surgical resection in colorectal endometriosis was observed.

Among 71 women with rectal endometriosis, there were no differences in postoperative pelvic pain between women undergoing rectal shaving vs. those undergoing colorectal resection. Women undergoing rectal shaving had significantly better Gastrointestinal Quality of Life Index values, lower scores for postoperative constipation, and better anal continence but rectal recurrence occurred in 8.7% of these patients.
However, a short term prospective RCT on laparoscopic anterior resection of rectum for deeply infiltrating rectal endometriosis among 29 patients showed short-term benefit of rapid symptom relief.
The current guidelines are consistent in stating that surgery improves fertility in patients with endometriosis‐associated subfertility.
Post‐operative LNG‐IUD is widely used to reduce endometriosis‐related pain and to improve operative outcomes, however there is no high‐quality evidence to support this practice.

Conservative surgery with adjunctive presacral neurectomy may provide greater relief from midline pain and a similarly low rate of operative complications relative to conservative surgery alone, but may increase the risk of constipation.

In a case series of 14 patients with primary or recurrent ovarian endometriomas, catheter-directed sclerotherapy with 95% ethanol resulted in pain relief in all women with no recurrences of endometrioma at one year. No procedure-related complications were reported and there were no differences in serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels before and 6 months after treatment, indicating preserved ovarian function.
Hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (HBSO)

HBSO is more definitive treatment, but there is no supporting evidence from RCTs. The recurrence of symptoms and pelvic pain are directly correlated to the surgical precision and removal of peritoneal and deeply infiltrated disease.

Compared to an excisional endometriosis surgery group, pain scores improved with combined EES-HBSO cohort by 2.106/10 at 6 months (95%CI 0.469-3.742, p=0.012), 2.642/10 at 12 months (95%CI 0.871-4.413, p=0.004), and 2.548/10 at 24 months (95%CI 0.681-4.414, p=0.008).

Authors of a Cochrane review of abdominal hysterectomy versus vaginal hysterectomy for benign gynecologic disease showed fewer complications, shorter hospital stay, and a quicker return to work with vaginal hysterectomy. Laparoscopic hysterectomy also resulted in a shorter hospital stay, decreased risk of wound/abdominal wall infection and transfusion, and quicker return to normal activities compared to abdominal hysterectomy, but was associated with increased risk of ureteric injury and longer operative time.

Low to moderate certainty evidence from 15 trials including 1018 patients showed manual acupuncture was more effective than sham acupuncture at reducing dysmenorrhea VAS pain score (mean difference [MD] - 2.40, 95 % CI [- 2.80, - 2.00]; pelvic pain VAS score (MD - 2.65, 95 % CI [- 3.40, - 1.90] and dyspareunia VAS scores (MD - 2.88, [- 3.83, - 1.93]), and improving quality of life. Other authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed the benefit of acupuncture on endometriosis symptoms. Authors of a Cochrane review found only a single trial of acupunture for endometriosis, in which aural acupuncture was more effective than Chinese Herbal Medicine (CHM) for reducing pain in severe dysmenorrhea.

In a Cochrane review (2 RCT, 158 women), postsurgical administration of CHM appears to have comparable benefits to gestrinone but with fewer side effects. However, CHM had better dysmenorrhea pain reduction than danazol when administered in conjunction with herbal enema. Neither trial compared CHM with placebo treatment.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 trials including 1052 women with endometriosis found Guizhi Fuling pill, a traditional Chinese herbal formula, plus mifepristone was superior to mifepristone alone in reducing endometriosis recurrence (RR 0.40; 95% CI 0.27-0.59) and improving pregnancy rates (RR 1.74; 95% confidence intervals [CI] 1.40-2.17). However, methodological flaws of the included trials was observed.

In a small RCT of 59 women with pelvic pain and a history of endometriosis or infertility, more women randomized to vitamins E and C for 8 weeks prior to planned surgery reported improvements in everyday pain, dysmenorrhea, and dyspareunia compared with the placebo group. In addition, there was a significant decrease in peritoneal fluid inflammatory markers for intervention vs. control women.
Supplementation of vitamin C 1000 mg/day and vitamin E 800 IU/da y for short duration of 8 weeks reduced the severity of pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea and improved dyspareunia in a small RCT.
In a double blind, placebo-controlled RCT, supplementation with vitamin D or omega 3 fatty acids led to similar improvment in pelvic pain as that observed in placebo arm.

In a study of 100 Chinese women with endometriosis receiving GnRH-agonist therapy, women randomized to 12 weeks of progressive muscle relaxation training had significantly greater improvements in measures of depression, anxiety, and overall quality of life compared to women in the control group.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 studies showed physical therapy improved pain intensity (SMD -0.89, 95% CI -1.21 to -0.57; I2 69%) and quality of life.

In two small RCTs of women with dysmenorrhea and laparoscopically-diagnosed endometriosis, perturbation (passing a solution through the uterine cavity and the Fallopian tubes via an intra-cervical balloon catheter) with lidocaine or Lignocaine resulted in a clinically significant reduction in dysmenorrhea over placebo. In the first cited trial, four of 9 women who had treatment success had a persistent effect at 9 months.
Pulsed laser treatment 3 times weekly for 8 weeks in addition to hormonal therapy was better with respect to pain than sham-laser treatment in an RCT of 40 women with endometriosis.

In a retrospective study of 83 Chinese women with endometriosis-associated pain who received neuromuscular electrical stimulation and were observed for 10 weeks compared to 71 wait-listed control subjects, no differences in symptoms as measured by the Endometriosis System Sevreity scale or quality of life were observed earlier at 5 weeks. Mild adverse effects of dizziness, discomfort, headache, muscle spasm, and itchy skin were reported by about 9.6% of women in the intervention group and 1 in the control group.
Referral is required for definitive diagnosis by laparoscopy.
Referral is required when treatment with danazol or GnRH analogs is needed but are outside the experience of the primary care provider.
Between 30% and 50% of women with endometriosis have some degree of infertility due to distortion of the fallopian tubes and impaired ovum release and pickup.
A leading cause of infertility, endometriosis has a prevalence of 0.5-5% in fertile and 25-40% in infertile women.

Based on a systematic review, women with and without endometriosis have comparable outcomes in terms of live births following ART; women with severe endometriosis, however, have a lower live-birth rate, clinical pregnancy rate, and mean number of oocytes retrieved when compared with women with no endometriosis.

Results from a meta-analysis of studies on woman undergoing IVF treatment showed that fertilization rates were reduced in stage I/II of endometriosis (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.87-0.99) and there was a decrease in implantation rate (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.67-0.93) and clinical pregnancy rate (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69-0.91) in women with stage III/IV endometriosis.

In one case-control study of women undergoing IVF, there was no difference in the number of live births to women with and without endometriomas (61 [78%] and 130 [83%], respectively) or for late pregnancy or neonatal outcomes. This rate of births is high compared to other reports; for example, among women with deep infiltrating endometriosis undergoing IVF in one case-series, the pregnancy rate was 58%.
The cumulative pregnancy rate (CPR) in the whole population after three ICSI-IVF cycles was 68.6%. The CPR for patients with or without associated adenomyosis was 19 and 82.4%, respectively (P= 0.01)

Among 308 women with endometriosis undergoing ART with intracytoplasmic sperm injection procedures, those randomized to laser-assisted hatching by thinning of the zona pellucida had higher clinical pregnancy rates than control women (29.1% vs. 18.7%, respectively); OR 1.79 (95% CI 1.05-3.06), NNT 9.57 (95% CI 5.03-98.99) and a trend towards higher live birth dates (25.3% vs. 16.7%, OR 1.69 (95% CI 0.97-2.97).

The Endometriosis Fertility Index (EFI) score is a validated 10-point scale system based on age at surgery, infertility duration in years, prior pregnancy, least function score, severity score for the patient and total severity score for all patients, ranging from 0 for the poorest prognosis to 10 for the best prognosis.

Based on the EFI scores, authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies with 4598 women found the cumulative non-ART pregnancy rate at 36 months was 10% (95% CI 3%-16%) for women with an EFI of 0 to 2, which significantly increased to 69% (95% CI 58%-79%) for women with an EFI of 9 to 10.The summary area under the curve (AUC) was 0.72.

In one study of 107 women who wished to conceive following surgery for recurrent endometriosis, women with an EFI score >5 had a 2-year cumulative pregnancy rate of 51.86% vs. 26% for women with EFI score <5.

In a retrospective study of 303 women with colorectal endometriosis managed by segmental resection or disc excision over 40 consecutive months, 7.9% developed pelvic abscess/infected hematoma and 2% developed bowel fistula. A CRP ≥100 mg/l at postoperative day 4 was associated with these early septic pelvic complications, with an AUC 0.85 (95% CI 0.78-0.92).

Authors of a discussion paper on surgical complications and their management listed diminished ovarian reserve as the most common complication of surgery for ovarian endometriomas. For deep infiltrating lesions of the bowel, complications include leakage at the anastomosis site (1% to 15% depending on location), rectal perforation (1.4% in one study), and ureter damage in <1%. For deep infiltrating lesions of the bladder and ureters, reported complications were fistulas, pyelonephritis, and bladder atony.
Endometriosis may resolve (25%) or stabilize (25%) without treatment in many premenopausal women.
As endometriosis is hormone dependent, it resolves post menopause.
Following laparoscopic excision, reported recurrence rates for endometrioma are between 11% and 32% within 1 to 5 years.
A Dutch population-based cohort study showed women with ovarian cancer and histologically proven-endometriosis had longer overall survival than women with ovarian cancer without endometriosis.

Based on a literature review, pregnant women with endometriosis have an increased risk of spontaneous hemoperitoneum. This condition is rare but associated with high fetal mortality (31%) as well as preterm birth (spontaneous pregnancy OR 1.37; 95% CI 1.24-1.5 or assisted pregnancy OR 1.24; 95% CI 0.99-1.57), placenta previa (OR 1.7; 95% CI 1.2-2.40), and postpartum hemorrhage (OR 1.3; 95% CI 1.1-1.6). Acute complications such as spontaneous hemoperitoneum, bowel and ovarian complications, represent rare but life-threatening conditions that require surgical operations in most cases.

In a study of 318 pregnancies conceived by ART, endometriosis was significantly associated with placenta previa (OR 15.1; 95% CI 7.6-500). Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies with 21,930 pregnancies including 6,256 women with endometriosis also found an increased risk of placenta previa among women with endometriosis (OR 4.04; 95% CI 2.29-7.12); a higher OR of 5.54, 95% CI 1.66-18.52 was found for women with endometriosis who conceived with ART.

In a meta-analysis of 9 cohort studies including 13,798 women with an endometriosis diagnosis, there was an increased risk of preterm birth (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.32-1.90 in women following spontaneous conception and OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.14-1.79 in women who conceived with ART).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 cohort and 4 case-control studies found that women with endometriosis, whether laparoscopically diagnosed or biopsy proven, did not have increased risks of preeclampsia, eclampsia or HELLP syndrome. However, in a recent systemic review, there was an increased risk of preeclampsia in women who conceived spontaneously (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.13 -1.89).

In a cohort study of 67 women with colorectal endometriosis, in-situ or post-surgical, who had 72 pregnancies, postoperative complications (e.g., postpartum hemorrhage, 4th degree tear, endometritis) occurred in 39% of the 36 women undergoing caesarean section and 14% of the 36 women after vaginal delivery.
There is an increased risk of impaired obstetric outcome in women with endometriosis during their first pregnancy, while a reduced number of complications occur in successive pregnancies.
